title: India Clears ₹1.1 Lakh Crore Defence Acquisition With 98% Sourced From Domestic Industry
excerpt: The Defence Acquisition Council approved procurement proposals spanning CBRN vehicles, marine gas turbines and advanced helicopters for all three services, with nearly all sourcing from Indian manufacturers.
body:
• The Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, approved capital acquisition proposals worth approximately ₹1.10 lakh crore ($11.6 billion) on September 7
  • About 98% of procurements by value will be sourced from Indian industry, reinforcing the government's push for indigenous defence manufacturing
  • Army approvals include CBRN reconnaissance vehicles, high mobility vehicles, mine layers, advanced light helicopters and the Sarvatra bridge system
  • Navy gets Arudhra radars and a programme to develop marine gas turbines domestically, reducing dependence on foreign propulsion suppliers

Biggest Defence Approval of the Year

India's Defence Acquisition Council on Monday gave in-principle approval to military acquisition proposals worth approximately ₹1.10 lakh crore ($11.6 billion) for the Army, Navy and Air Force, with about 98% of the procurements to be sourced from Indian industry, the Ministry of Defence said.

https://x.com/SpokespersonMoD/status/2097007230407315665

The approvals — known as Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) — were granted at a meeting chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on September 7. An AoN is the initial administrative approval for a proposed acquisition; projects still require tendering, technical evaluation, price negotiations and final contractual approval before hardware starts arriving.

What the Army Gets

For the Indian Army, the approved proposals include Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) reconnaissance vehicles that can detect, identify, monitor and mark contaminated areas. The ministry also cleared High Mobility Vehicles for troop mobility in difficult terrain, Self-Propelled Mechanical Mine Layers for faster mine-laying capability, and the Sarvatra Bridge System for combat formations to establish crossings during operations.

Advanced Light Helicopters were approved for both the Army and the Indian Air Force to support complex missions across diverse terrains and operational conditions.

Navy and Air Force Modernisation

The Indian Navy received clearance for Arudhra radars that will replace existing air-route surveillance systems at naval air stations. More significantly, the DAC approved the design, development and subsequent procurement of Marine Gas Turbines — a move intended to reduce India's dependence on foreign vendors for warship propulsion systems.

"Approximately 98 per cent of the approved procurement by value would be sourced from Indian industry."

— Ministry of Defence statement

For the Air Force, approvals included ground-based multi-purpose jammers and a radio-frequency identification-based Defence Forces Secure Access Card system, alongside projects to strengthen fighter, transport and helicopter fleet capabilities. The ministry did not disclose the value, quantity or delivery schedule for individual proposals.

The Make in India Defence Push

The 98% domestic sourcing target is the most striking feature of these approvals. It reflects the government's sustained push for self-reliance in defence manufacturing under the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative. The DAC had cleared a smaller ₹52,000 crore tranche in July and a ₹1.05 lakh crore package in July 2025, establishing a pattern of large-scale indigenous procurement.

India's defence industry has been one of the fastest-growing sectors for private manufacturers, with companies like Bharat Electronics, Hindustan Aeronautics and a growing roster of private firms competing for contracts. For Indian-origin defence technology professionals abroad, the expanding pipeline represents potential opportunities in both Indian operations and export markets.

What's Next

The approved proposals will now move to detailed requirements, requests for proposals and contracting. The marine gas turbine programme in particular will be watched closely — domestic warship propulsion has long been a gap in India's defence manufacturing capability, and success here would mark a significant milestone in reducing reliance on foreign suppliers.
